wiki_only_topics.topic: Etymology and linguistic derivation of Hindustan from Persian and Sanskrit.
wiki_only_topics.quote_wikipedia: Hindustan is derived from the Persian word Hindū, which is cognate with the Sanskrit word Sindhu (meaning " Indus River "). The Proto-Iranian sound change *s > h occurred between 850 and 600 BCE, according to Asko Parpola.

wiki_only_topics.topic: Historical distinction between Hindustan and Hind during the Delhi Sultanate and Mughal Empire.
wiki_only_topics.quote_wikipedia: In the time of the Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526) and the Mughal Empire (1526–1857), the ruling elite and its Persian historiographers made a further distinction between "Hindustan" and "Hind". Hindustan referred to the territories of northern India in the Doab and adjacent regions under Muslim political control, while "Hind" referred to the rest of India.

wiki_only_topics.topic: Usage of Hindustan during the Indian independence movement and partition of 1947.
wiki_only_topics.quote_wikipedia: The 1940 Lahore Resolution of the All-India Muslim League demanded sovereignty for the Muslim-majority areas in the northwest and northeast of British India, which came to be called ' Pakistan ' in popular parlance and the Dominion of India came to be called 'Hindustan'.

wiki_only_topics.topic: The Hindustani language and its literary standards (Hindi and Urdu).
wiki_only_topics.quote_wikipedia: The Hindustani language is the language of Hindustan and the lingua franca of the northern Indian subcontinent. Hindustani derives from the Old Hindi language of Western Uttar Pradesh and Delhi areas. Its literary standard forms— Modern Standard Hindi and Modern Standard Urdu —use different scripts.

wiki_only_topics.topic: Use of 'Jai Hind' by the Indian Armed Forces.
wiki_only_topics.quote_wikipedia: The Indian Armed Forces use the salutary version of the name, " Jai Hind ", as a battle cry.
